<h1>Overview</h1>
</header>
<p>
Casbin is an efficient, open-source access control library that enforces authorization and supports multiple 
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Access_control#Access_control_models" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="">access control models</a>
.
</p>
<p>
Implementing rule-based access control is straightforward: define subjects, objects, and permitted actions in a 
<strong>
<em>policy</em>
</strong>
 file in any format that fits your needs. This pattern is consistent across all Casbin implementations. The 
<strong>
<em>model</em>
</strong>
 file gives developers and administrators full control over authorization logic—layout, execution flow, and conditions. The 
<strong>
<em>Enforcer</em>
</strong>
 component evaluates incoming requests against your model and policy.
</p>

<h2 class="anchor anchorTargetHideOnScrollNavbar_vjPI" id="what-is-casbin">
What is Casbin?
<a href="#what-is-casbin" class="hash-link" aria-label="Direct link to What is Casbin?" title="Direct link to What is Casbin?" translate="no">
​
</a>
</h2>
<p>
Casbin is an authorization library for applications that need controlled access to resources. Typically, a 
<strong>subject</strong>
 (user or service) requests access to an 
<strong>object</strong>
 (resource or entity) to perform an 
<strong>action</strong>
 (e.g. 
<em>read</em>
, 
<em>write</em>
, or 
<em>delete</em>
). You define these actions to match your application. This is the standard 
<code>{ subject, object, action }</code>
 flow that Casbin handles most often.
</p>
<p>
Casbin also supports more complex scenarios through 
<a class="" href="/docs/rbac">roles (RBAC)</a>
, 
<a class="" href="/docs/abac">attributes (ABAC)</a>
, and other patterns.
</p>
<h3 class="anchor anchorTargetHideOnScrollNavbar_vjPI" id="what-casbin-does">
What Casbin Does
<a href="#what-casbin-does" class="hash-link" aria-label="Direct link to What Casbin Does" title="Direct link to What Casbin Does" translate="no">
​
</a>
</h3>
<ol>
<li class="">
<strong>Enforces policy</strong>
 in the classic 
<code>{ subject, object, action }</code>
 format or any custom format you define, including both allow and deny.
</li>
<li class="">
<strong>Manages storage</strong>
 for the access control model and policies.
</li>
<li class="">
<strong>Handles user–role and role–role relationships</strong>
 (RBAC role hierarchy).
</li>
<li class="">
<strong>Supports built-in superusers</strong>
 (e.g. 
<code>root</code>
, 
<code>administrator</code>
) with unrestricted access without explicit rules.
</li>
<li class="">
<strong>Provides built-in operators</strong>
 for pattern matching (e.g. 
<code>keyMatch</code>
 matches 
<code>/foo/bar</code>
 against 
<code>/foo*</code>
).
</li>
</ol>
<h3 class="anchor anchorTargetHideOnScrollNavbar_vjPI" id="what-casbin-does-not-do">
What Casbin Does Not Do
<a href="#what-casbin-does-not-do" class="hash-link" aria-label="Direct link to What Casbin Does Not Do" title="Direct link to What Casbin Does Not Do" translate="no">
​
</a>
</h3>
<ol>
<li class="">
<strong>User authentication</strong>
 — validating usernames and passwords at login.
</li>
<li class="">
<strong>User or role list management</strong>
 — maintaining the list of users or roles.
</li>
</ol>
<p>Most applications already manage users, roles, and credentials. Casbin focuses only on authorization and does not store or verify passwords. In RBAC mode, it does maintain user–role associations.</p>
